title: How to Plan Retirement When One Spouse Doesn’t Work
description: Securing the future for stay-at-home partners.
content:
In single-income households, retirement planning carries an extra layer of risk. The working spouse is the sole engine of wealth, but two people need to survive on the nest egg. If the earner dies or becomes disabled, the non-working spouse is often left vulnerable. Financial planning for this dynamic requires aggressive use of 'Spousal' accounts, robust life insurance, and a clear understanding of Survivor benefits. This guide explains how to build a safety net for two on one salary.

Key Takeaways

  • Spousal IRA: Even if a spouse has $0 income, the working spouse can contribute to a 'Spousal IRA' (Traditional or Roth) in their name. This effectively doubles the household's IRA space to $14,000/year.
  • Life Insurance is Mandatory: You need 10-15x the earner's salary in Term Life insurance. If the earner dies at 50, the non-working spouse needs a bridge to Social Security age.
  • Social Security Spousal Benefit: A non-working spouse is entitled to 50% of the earner's benefit at Full Retirement Age. If the earner gets $3,000, the spouse gets $1,500. Total: $4,500.
  • Survivor Planning: If the earner dies in retirement, the household loses one Social Security check (the smaller one). Ensure the portfolio is large enough to cover the income drop.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Divorce laws vary by state, but retirement assets accumulated during marriage are generally split 50/50. However, establishing credit and assets in the non-working spouse's name is a critical safety measure for their financial autonomy.

The Protection Architecture

Protect the non-earner at all costs.

1. Maximize Spousal Accounts

Action: Fully fund the Spousal Roth IRA ($7,000) every year.
Why: This builds a bucket of money legally owned by the non-working spouse. It provides autonomy and tax-free growth.

2. The Pension Decision

If the earner has a pension, they must choose a payout option.
Single Life: Higher check, stops at death.
Joint & Survivor: Lower check, continues for spouse.
Verdict: Always choose Joint & Survivor unless you have massive life insurance. Do not leave the spouse penniless.

3. Disability Insurance

If the earner breaks their back, the income stops. 'Own Occupation' disability insurance replaces 60% of income. This is more important than the 401(k) match.

The 'Return to Work' Plan

  1. Skill Maintenance: The non-working spouse should keep certifications active or volunteer. This reduces 're-entry friction' if they need to return to the workforce suddenly.
  2. Establish Credit: Ensure the non-working spouse has a credit card in their own name (as primary account holder), not just as an authorized user. They need a credit score.
  3. The 'Widow's Budget': Run a simulation. If the earner dies, what does life look like? Can the survivor afford the house? If not, more insurance is needed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can we retire early?

It is harder on one income. You need a savings rate of 30-40%. It requires a high income or low expenses. But the Spousal IRA helps significantly.

What if we divorce?

The non-working spouse is usually entitled to half the marital assets (401k/house) and potentially alimony. But the best protection is having your own accounts.

Does the non-earner get Medicare?

Yes. If the working spouse qualifies (40 quarters of work), the non-working spouse qualifies for Medicare at 65 based on the earner's record.
